title: One From Each Set
statement:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ be non-empty finite sets such that
$$\dfrac{1}{|A_1|} + \dfrac{1}{|A_2|} + \dots + \dfrac{1}{|A_n|} \le 1.$$
Prove that there are at least $n!$ ordered $n$-tuples $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$ such that $a_i \in A_i$ for every $i$ and the elements $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are pairwise distinct.
hints: Number the sets so that $|A_1| \le |A_2| \le \dots \le |A_n|$ and choose $a_1$, then $a_2$, and so on. Bound the number of choices at each step from below, and look at what happens when all the sets are the same set of $n$ elements.

With $x_k = |A_k|$ the count is at least $\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x_k - k + 1)$, so it suffices to show that this product is at least $n!$. Put $t_k = \frac{1}{x_k}$ and write $x_k - k + 1 = \frac{1}{t_k}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right)$. The AM-GM inequality bounds the product of the numbers $\frac{1}{t_k}$. For the other product, use the weighted AM-GM inequality after writing $(t_1, \dots, t_n)$ as a weighted average of simpler vectors.

As $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \ge t_n$, the weights $\lambda_i = i(t_i - t_{i+1})$ for $1 \le i \le n$, with $t_{n+1} = 0$, and $\lambda_0 = 1 - (t_1 + \dots + t_n)$ are non-negative with sum $1$, and $t_k = \sum_{i=k}^{n}\frac{\lambda_i}{i}$. So $(t_1, \dots, t_n)$ is a weighted average of the zero vector and the vectors whose first $i$ entries are $\frac{1}{i}$ and whose other entries are $0$. Apply the weighted AM-GM inequality to each $1 - (k-1)t_k$ written in this way, and compute the product over $k$ for each of these vectors.
solution: Write $x_i = |A_i|$ and call an $n$-tuple as in the statement good. Renumbering the sets permutes the coordinates of every good $n$-tuple, so it does not change their number, and we may number the sets so that $x_1 \le x_2 \le \dots \le x_n$. Let $$P = \prod_{k=1}^{n}(x_k - k + 1).$$ Counting. For $1 \le k \le n$ the sizes $x_1, \dots, x_k$ are at most $x_k$, so $\frac{k}{x_k} \le \frac{1}{x_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{x_k} \le 1$. Hence $x_k \ge k$, and every factor $x_k - k + 1$ of $P$ is at least $1$. For $0 \le k \le n$ let $N_k$ be the number of $k$-tuples $(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ of pairwise distinct elements with $a_j \in A_j$ for every $j \le k$, so that $N_0 = 1$ and $N_n$ is the number of good $n$-tuples. A $k$-tuple of this kind with $k < n$ can be extended by any element of $A_{k+1}$ other than $a_1, \dots, a_k$, so it has at least $x_{k+1} - k$ extensions, and different $k$-tuples have different extensions. Hence $N_{k+1} \ge (x_{k+1} - k)\,N_k$ for $0 \le k < n$. All these factors are positive, so chaining the $n$ inequalities gives $N_n \ge P\,N_0 = P$, and it suffices to prove that $P \ge n!$. Splitting the product. Put $t_k = \frac{1}{x_k}$. Then $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \ge t_n > 0$, $t_1 + t_2 + \dots + t_n \le 1$ and $$x_k - k + 1 = \dfrac{1}{t_k}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right).$$ By the AM-GM inequality, $\left(t_1 t_2 \cdots t_n\right)^{1/n} \le \frac{1}{n}\left(t_1 + \dots + t_n\right) \le \frac{1}{n}$, so $$\prod_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{t_k} \ge n^n. \qquad (1)$$ A weighted average. Let $t_{n+1} = 0$, let $\lambda_i = i(t_i - t_{i+1})$ for $1 \le i \le n$, and let $\lambda_0 = 1 - (t_1 + \dots + t_n)$. These numbers are non-negative, and $$\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots + \lambda_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i\,t_i - \sum_{i=2}^{n}(i-1)\,t_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_i,$$ so $\lambda_0 + \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n = 1$. Moreover $t_k = \sum_{i=k}^{n}(t_i - t_{i+1}) = \sum_{i=k}^{n}\frac{\lambda_i}{i}$, and therefore $$1 - (k-1)t_k = \sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_i\,c_{ik}, \qquad c_{ik} = \begin{cases} 1 - \dfrac{k-1}{i} & \text{if } i \ge k, \\ 1 & \text{if } i < k. \end{cases}$$ For $i \ge k$ we have $c_{ik} \ge 1 - \frac{i-1}{i} = \frac{1}{i}$, so every $c_{ik}$ is positive. The second product. For each $k$, the weighted AM-GM inequality with weights $\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ gives $$1 - (k-1)t_k \ge \prod_{i=0}^{n} c_{ik}^{\lambda_i},$$ where a factor with $\lambda_i = 0$ equals $1$. Multiplying these $n$ inequalities, $$\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right) \ge \prod_{i=0}^{n} g_i^{\lambda_i}, \qquad \text{where } g_i = \prod_{k=1}^{n} c_{ik}.$$ Here $g_0 = 1$, and for $1 \le i \le n$ only the factors with $k \le i$ differ from $1$, so $$g_i = \prod_{k=1}^{i}\dfrac{i - k + 1}{i} = \dfrac{i!}{i^i}.$$ Since $\frac{g_{i+1}}{g_i} = \left(\frac{i}{i+1}\right)^{i} < 1$ for $i \ge 1$ and $g_0 = g_1 = 1$, every $g_i$ with $0 \le i \le n$ satisfies $g_i \ge g_n = \frac{n!}{n^n} > 0$. As $\lambda_i \ge 0$, each $g_i^{\lambda_i}$ is at least $g_n^{\lambda_i}$, and the weights add up to $1$, so $$\prod_{i=0}^{n} g_i^{\lambda_i} \ge g_n^{\lambda_0 + \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n} = g_n,$$ and hence $$\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right) \ge \dfrac{n!}{n^n}. \qquad (2)$$ Multiplying (1) and (2) gives $P \ge n!$, so there are at least $n!$ good $n$-tuples. If every $A_i$ is the same set of $n$ elements, there are exactly $n!$, so the bound cannot be improved. Remark. For nested sets $A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \dots \subseteq A_n$ the number of good $n$-tuples is exactly $P$, so the problem is equivalent to the inequality $P \ge n!$. A comparison factor by factor fails, since $x_1$ may be $2$. So does an induction on $n$ that bounds $P$ below by one of its factors times $(n-1)!$, since this gives $n!$ only when that factor is at least $n$: for the sizes $3, 4, 5, 6$ every factor of $P$ equals $3$, which is less than $n = 4$. Another route to (2) is majorisation. The same weights show that any $j$ of the numbers $(k-1)t_k$ have sum at most the sum of the $j$ largest of $\frac{0}{n}, \frac{1}{n}, \dots, \frac{n-1}{n}$, and the weak form of Karamata's inequality for the convex increasing function $-\log(1 - x)$ then gives (2).

rubric.criterion: Orders the sets by size and proves that the number of good $n$-tuples is at least $\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x_k - k + 1)$, where $x_1 \le x_2 \le \dots \le x_n$ are the sizes, or an equivalent reduction to an inequality about the sizes alone. Deduct 1 if the bounds for the successive choices are multiplied together without a proof that $x_k \ge k$ for every $k$, which makes every factor positive, for example because the sets were not ordered by size before the choices were counted.

Splits each factor as $\frac{1}{t_k}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right)$ with $t_k = \frac{1}{x_k}$, or as $x_k\left(1 - \frac{k-1}{x_k}\right)$, proves that $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n \ge n^n$, and so reduces the problem to $\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right) \ge \frac{n!}{n^n}$.

Writes $(t_1, \dots, t_n)$ as a weighted average of the zero vector and the vectors whose first $i$ entries are $\frac{1}{i}$, with weights $i(t_i - t_{i+1})$, or proves an equivalent majorisation or concavity statement that reduces the remaining product to these vectors.

Proves $\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right) \ge \frac{n!}{n^n}$, for example by the weighted AM-GM inequality and the fact that $\frac{i!}{i^i}$ decreases, and concludes that there are at least $n!$ good $n$-tuples. Deduct 1 if it is not shown that $\frac{i!}{i^i}$ decreases. A complete proof by another route earns all marks.

milestones.criterion: Orders the sets by size and proves that the number of good $n$-tuples is at least $\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x_k - k + 1)$, or an equivalent reduction. Deduct 1 if the bounds for the successive choices are multiplied together without a proof that $x_k \ge k$ for every $k$, which makes every factor positive.
Proves $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n \ge n^n$ and reduces the problem to $\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1 - (k-1)t_k\right) \ge \frac{n!}{n^n}$ with $t_k = \frac{1}{x_k}$.
Proves that for every $j$, any $j$ of the numbers $(k-1)t_k$ have sum at most the sum of the $j$ largest of $\frac{0}{n}, \frac{1}{n}, \dots, \frac{n-1}{n}$.
Applies the weak form of Karamata's inequality to the convex increasing function $-\log(1 - x)$, or an equivalent argument, and concludes.

fatal_errors.error: Asserts without proof that $\prod (x_k - k + 1)$ is smallest when all the $x_k$ are equal, for example by symmetry or by a smoothing step that is not justified under the ordering $x_1 \le \dots \le x_n$.
Compares the factors one by one, for example claims $x_k - k + 1 \ge n - k + 1$ for every $k$, which fails when $x_1 < n$, or proves the bound only when every set has at least $n$ elements.

Proves $\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x_k - k + 1) \ge n!$ but proves that the number of good $n$-tuples is at least this product only for nested sets $A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \dots \subseteq A_n$, or assumes without proof that the sets may be taken to be nested.
